Getting to Know
Mutual Funds
What is a Mutual Fund?
A mutual fund is a collective investment option
where money from multiple investors like you is
pooled together and invested across equity,
money market instruments and other liquid
instruments, gold and silver instruments and in
invITs. This pooled money is managed by
professional fund managers, who invest it
according to the scheme's investment objective,
and you must make sure it aligns with your own
investment goals as well.
What happens when you
invest money in a Mutual Fund?
When you invest money in a mutual fund, the fund
issues “units” to you against the amount invested
at the prevailing NAV. Speaking of NAV (Net
Asset Value), it's the price you pay per unit to
invest in a mutual fund scheme.
Wondering why you should
invest in Mutual Funds?
Mutual funds allow you to invest in a wide
range of assets such as equity, money market
instruments and other liquid instruments, gold
and silver instruments and in invITs. They
provide an opportunity for retail investors like you
to participate in capital markets without having to
manage investments on your own.
Over the long term, investing can help your money
grow and potentially beat inflation, helping you
preserve its purchasing power. It can also help you
plan for and work towards your financial goals.
01

02
Well-regulated and
time-tested
Mutual funds in India are regulated by
SEBI, ensuring transparency and investor
protection.
Tax benefits
Investment in ELSS up to /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN1,50,000

of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Additionally,
mutual fund investments are tax-efficient
when held for the long term.
Professional

Your investments are managed by
experienced professionals who research
and monitor securities and invest on your
behalf.
Risk

Your money is spread across multiple
assets, so if any asset performs poorly,
others can help balance the impact,
reducing overall risk.
Affordability &
convenience
Mutual funds are accessible and easy, as
you can start investing with small amounts.
Liquidity
Open-ended funds can be redeemed on
any business day, with proceeds credited
within 1–3 working days (depending on the
scheme), while close-ended funds can be
redeemed only at maturity.

Risks in
Mutual Funds
Mutual funds are market-linked investments and involve certain risks. Returns are not guaranteed, and
the value of investments can fluctuate due to market movements, interest rate changes, credit events,
or economic factors.
Three risks you must be aware of before investing in mutual funds are
Market risk, meaning
the value of the fund
moves up and down
with changes in stock
and bond markets.
Loss of capital, where
there's the possible risk
of getting back less than
what you invested.
Liquidity risk, where
some investments may
be less liquid, making
them harder to sell
quickly when needed.
For more information, visit amfiindia.com/investor.

Other risks of investing in Mutual Fund include
interest-rate risk, credit/default risk and concentration risk.

Common Terms related to
Mutual Fund Investing
What is NAV?
NAV (Net Asset Value) is the price of one unit of a mutual fund.
It is calculated at the end of each trading day after market closes by
subtracting total liabilities from total assets and dividing by outstanding
units; it is the price you pay to buy or redeem units, subject to applicable
cut-off times and regulatory conditions.
What is an Exit Load?
Exit load is a fee charged when you redeem mutual fund units and is
deducted from the NAV at the time of redemption.
For instance, if the NAV is /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN100 and the exit load is 1%, the redemption
price would be /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN99 per unit.
What is Base expense ratio?
Base Expense Ratio (BER) refers to the core recurring expenses
associated with managing and operating a mutual fund scheme. It is the
sum of investment and advisory fees, marketing and selling expenses
including fees, commission and charges towards distribution of mutual
fund schemes if any, administrative and operating expenses and
scheme servicing and recurring management costs.
What is Total expense ratio?
Total Expense Ratio (TER) represents the complete cost of investing,
which adds external costs like brokerage, transaction fees, and
statutory levies to the base fee.
TER = Base Expense Ratio (BER) + Brokerage Cost + Transaction Cost
incurred for the purpose of execution of trade + Statutory levies
(including GST)

Systematic modes of investing
18
Modes of Investing
in Mutual Funds
How can you invest in Mutual Funds?
A lump-sum investment involves investing a large
amount of money in one go. Your money gets
invested immediately, and returns depend on
market conditions at the time of investment. Over
the long term, this can help you benefit from the
power of compounding.
If you have surplus funds, a long-term investment
horizon, and are comfortable with higher risk or
have a willingness to stay invested during market
downturns, then lump-sum investments would be
suitable for you.
Lump-sum investment
STP (Systematic Transfer Plan)
Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) is an option that
allows you to systematically transfer a fixed amount
from one mutual fund scheme to another, usually
from a debt fund to an equity fund, at regular
intervals. It helps you systematically transfer money
into the market, aiming to reduce the risk of market
timing while ensuring disciplined investing.
SIP (Systematic Investment Plan)
Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) is an
investment option offered by mutual funds where
you invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund
scheme at regular intervals — for example, daily,
weekly, monthly, etc. The SIP instalment amount
can be as low as /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN250-/uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN500 per month. It is also
a convenient way to invest in mutual funds, as
you can set up auto-debit from your bank
account for the instalments.

Power of Compounding

Compounding is when your money earns returns,
and those returns start earning returns too. Over
time, this creates a snowball effect, where even
small, regular investments can grow significantly.
For example, investing /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN1,000 every month at an
average return of 10% over 25 years can grow into
around /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN13.38 Lakh, even though you invested
only /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN3 lakh.
With the power of compounding, time does the
heavy lifting; you just need to be patient.

SIPs
SIP stands for Systematic Investment Plan, and
it allows you to invest small amounts regularly in
a mutual fund scheme instead of investing a
large sum at once. By investing consistently, you
benefit from the power of compounding and
rupee cost averaging, too.
SIPs have become popular as they enable you
to build wealth step by step, making investing
simple, disciplined, and easy on the pocket.
What is SIP , and why is it popular?

Rupee Cost Averaging
With SIPs, you invest the same amount regularly,
no matter how the market moves. This means you
buy more units when prices are low and fewer
units when prices are high. Over time, this helps
average out your purchase cost.
For example, a SIP of /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN1,000 gets you 50 units
when the NAV is /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN20, but 100 units when the NAV
is /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN10. The average cost for buying those 150 units
would be /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN2,000 ÷ 150 units, i.e., /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN13.33.
While it doesn't guarantee profits or prevent
losses, it encourages regular investing and helps
you avoid emotional decisions during market ups
and downs.

Cost of Delay: Why Starting Early is Important
When it comes to investing, time matters more than
the amount. Starting early gives your money more
time to grow through compounding, while delaying
investments can significantly reduce your wealth.
For example, consider two friends who both invest
a total of /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN21 lakh.
Delaying investments means losing out on those
extra years of growth, which can never be
recovered later. The lesson is simple: start early,
stay invested, and let time do the work for you.

Goal-based
Investing
Goal-based investing is an approach to wealth management where you invest money with a specific
purpose in mind, such as:
Instead of investing randomly, you first define your goal, time horizon, and risk comfort, and then choose
investments that align with that goal. This helps you stay focused, invest in a disciplined manner, and track
progress more clearly, making it easier to achieve your financial goals on time.
In short, you don't just invest money; you invest for a reason.

How Can Mutual Funds Help You Achieve Your Financial Goals?
Mutual Funds can be aligned with specific life goals by choosing schemes
based on your time horizon and risk profile. These goals may include:
Financial Independence
Financial independence as a goal means
building enough savings and investments so
that your regular expenses can be met without
depending on any active income. The aim is to
reach a stage where money provides stability,
freedom, and choices, allowing you to work
because you want to, not because you have to.
Planning for Child's Education
Child education planning focuses on saving
and investing for your child's future education,
such as higher studies or professional courses.
Since education costs increase over time,
planning early helps you manage these
expenses comfortably and reduces the need
for loans or financial stress later.
Retirement Planning
Retirement planning is about building a financial
cushion for your golden years. It helps ensure
you can maintain your lifestyle, manage
healthcare expenses, and meet everyday
needs without depending on others. By
investing regularly and starting early, you give
your money enough time to grow and support
you during your non-earning years.

23
What is
Redemption?
A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) allows you to withdraw a fixed amount at regular intervals, such as
monthly or quarterly from your mutual fund investment. Instead of redeeming the entire amount at once,
SWP provides a steady income, making it useful for goals like retirement or regular expenses.
SWP is simply a structured way to redeem, instead of withdrawing the full amount in one shot, it lets you set
up regular, automatic partial redemptions.
₹10 Lakh in a
Mutual Fund SWP of /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN20,000 per month
Disclaimer: The amounts are for illustrative purposes only.
What is an SWP?
For example:
You invest /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN10 lakh in a mutual fund scheme and set up an SWP of /uni20B9.INDIAN_RUPEE_SIGN20,000 per month. Every month, this
amount is credited to your bank account while the remaining corpus continues to remain invested and may
generate returns; the corpus may increase or decrease depending on investment performance and
withdrawals.
Withdraw
Redemption means withdrawing or selling your
mutual fund units. When you redeem, your units
are sold at the applicable NAV, and the
proceeds are credited to your bank account.
Depending on the scheme, an exit load or tax
may apply, especially if you redeem before the
specified period.
You can redeem your entire investment at once,
or in parts, whenever and however much you
need.

SCORES
(SEBI COmplaint REdressal System)
SCORES is an online grievance redressal
facilitation platform provided by SEBI that allows
you to file, track, and resolve complaints against
stock brokers, listed companies, mutual funds,
or other SEBI-registered intermediaries.
What Should You Do If You Have a Complaint?
You should first raise your grievance with the concerned entity, through its designated officials who handle
compliance and investor grievance matters.
If the issue remains unresolved, you can use the SCORES web portal (scores.sebi.gov.in) or the mobile app
to lodge your complaint and monitor its status online.
MITRA
(Mutual Fund Investment Tracing and Receiving Assitant)
Mitra is a Service platform for investors to
trace inactive and unclaimed Mutual Fund
folios- MITRA.
Login to MITRA portal on MF Central
to trace your inactive folios
or unclaimed investments:
https://app.mfcentral.com/links/mitra

SEBI
Saarthi App
The SEBI Saarthi App is a free personal finance and investment education app
